public_rationale: On May 6, 2026, Zillow reported 40% more code per engineer, unchanged or improved quality, and faster feature development [e1]. Its June 25 account described one employee's experiments taking a day instead of a two-week sprint, but falls outside the April 1–May 26 assessment period [e2]. These company accounts offer opposing evidence but do not establish comparable delivery and stability outcomes across heavy LLM users [e1, e2]. Neither account establishes or refutes the alleged 29,000 additional monthly human review hours or multimillion-dollar annualized AI coding spending at Zillow [e1, e2].
limitations: The internal deck, review-time definitions and baseline were not obtained or independently verified.
No independent records establish the claimed review burden or 2026 annualized spending.
Code volume does not measure useful software delivery, and the later employee account cannot establish company-wide April–May results.
Comparable target-period delivery and reliability measurements across the organizations covered by the claim are missing.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Heavy LLM code generation has not improved software output and brings stability problems; at Zillow it added 29,000 reviewer hours a month.

statement.excerpt: The answer is simple: they don’t know because nothing has actually changed. Organizations writing massive amounts of code using LLMs are facing massive product stability issues and, in the case of Zillow, spending millions of dollars a year to turn their codebase into a confusing, intentionless slop and increasing software reviewer loads by 29,000 hours a month.

from_speaker: Organizations writing massive amounts of code using LLMs
spending millions of dollars a year
increasing software reviewer loads by 29,000 hours a month
our_interpretation: Read the broad allegation as a lack of improvement in useful software delivery accompanied by serious reliability problems. Code volume alone does not measure useful output.
Read 29,000 hours as an incremental monthly human review burden caused by added code, rather than total review time, elapsed pull-request time or a hypothetical projection.
Treat descriptions such as 'slop' as rhetoric; assess defects, maintainability, delivery and review labor.
For ongoing operations, use the latest complete month before publication and the current period through publication.

The linked background article presents annual spending as an extrapolation from current spending. The monetary component is therefore an annualized estimate for 2026, not a completed year's expenditure.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable engineering records show no useful delivery improvement and serious stability problems at the organizations invoked, while Zillow records establish an additional 29,000 human review hours per month and multimillion-dollar annualized AI spending.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable outcome records show material delivery improvements without the alleged deterioration, or Zillow's underlying records establish that the 29,000-hour figure is incorrect or measures something other than incremental monthly human review labor.

evidence.locator: Section 'Six months ago, Zach Harrison didn’t trust AI tools'
evidence.explanation: Zillow provides a concrete employee account of faster experimentation. Its later date and limited scope prevent treating it as decisive evidence about April–May company-wide outcomes.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Authenticated Zillow review records identifying the month, baseline, active human review time and attribution to LLM-generated code; records supporting or refuting the 2026 annualized spending estimate; and comparable delivery and reliability measurements across the organizations invoked for April 1–May 26, 2026.
